title: Noam Chomsky vs. Michel Foucault: Human Nature — Justice versus Power (Eindhoven, November 1971)
context: Authentic philosophical reconstruction of the landmark televised debate between linguist and analytic rationalist Noam Chomsky and French post-structuralist philosopher Michel Foucault, moderated by Dutch philosopher Fons Elders at the Eindhoven University of Technology in November 1971. Follows the full 5-round arc: (1) the ontological existence of 'human nature' vs. historical nominalism, (2) Cartesian innate cognitive schema and generative grammar vs. the archaeology of knowledge and historical epistemes, (3) institutional power, psychiatric/penal normalization, and regimes of truth, (4) universal rational justice vs. justice as an instrument of class power, and (5) proletarian revolution, anarcho-syndicalism, and political action.

metadata.event: International Philosophers Project Debate: Human Nature — Justice versus Power
metadata.location: Eindhoven University of Technology, Eindhoven, Netherlands
key_themes: Innate Human Nature vs. Historical Episteme
metadata.historical_outcome: Exposed an irreconcilable philosophical divergence ('tunnellers working from opposite sides of the mountain'): Chomsky grounded politics in universal human nature and justice, while Foucault unmasked justice and truth as historically contingent effects of institutional power.

turns.speaker: Fons Elders
turns.text: Welcome, Professor Chomsky and Professor Foucault, to Eindhoven for tonight's philosophical dialogue on 'Human Nature: Justice versus Power.' Perhaps the best way to understand your encounter is to see both philosophers as tunnellers digging through opposite sides of the same mountain with very different tools, without yet knowing whether your paths meet. Let us begin with the fundamental question: does there exist an innate, universal human nature, or is human consciousness wholly produced by history and language?

turns.speaker: Noam Chomsky
turns.text: A person studying human language confronts a remarkably clear empirical problem: an adult speaker acquires an extraordinary creative capacity to say what he means and understand infinitely many novel sentences on the basis of very limited, degenerate childhood experience. That creative linguistic competence cannot be explained by blank-slate conditioning; it requires an innate, biologically given human nature—a rich cognitive schema of universal grammar fixed in the human mind as part of our biological endowment.

turns.speaker: Michel Foucault
turns.text: I must confess a deep skepticism toward the concept of 'human nature' as an explanatory foundation. In the history of the sciences—biology, medicine, economics, and philology—concepts such as 'life,' 'man,' and 'human nature' have served primarily as epistemological indicators marking boundaries of discourse within a particular period rather than timeless biological essences. Rather than beginning from an abstract human nature, I analyze the unconscious rules and historical conditions under which knowledge itself becomes possible.

turns.speaker: Fons Elders
turns.text: Notice how sharply your methods diverge in Round 2: Professor Chomsky seeks deep innate cognitive structures inside the individual mind, while Professor Foucault looks across historical epochs for anonymous epistemic transformations. How do you reconcile cognitive schema with the historical episteme?

turns.speaker: Noam Chomsky
turns.text: I see no contradiction between recognizing historical shifts in scientific paradigms and insisting on an invariant cognitive schema that makes creative inquiry possible in the first place. Just as Descartes and Humboldt observed, normal human language exhibits rule-governed creativity free from immediate stimulus control. Without a constraining innate mental structure, a child or a scientist could never bridge the gulf between sparse data and coherent theories—just as scientific creativity requires fixed innate principles to generate new discoveries.

turns.speaker: Michel Foucault
turns.text: Yet when I examine the transition from the classical seventeenth-century episteme to modern biology or political economy, I am struck not by the creative genius of an invariant Cartesian subject, but by sudden anonymous ruptures in the order of knowledge. What counts as rational perception, scientific truth, or madness is governed by rules external to individual consciousness—a positive unconscious of knowledge that reshapes what subjects can even think or perceive across historical periods.

turns.speaker: Fons Elders
turns.text: Let us move from epistemology to society in Round 3. How do neutral-appearing social institutions—universities, science, courts, psychiatry, and the state—shape power and human creativity?

turns.speaker: Michel Foucault
turns.text: In a society such as ours, power is never confined solely to explicit political rulers or economic ownership; it operates continuously through institutions that claim to be neutral, independent, and purely scientific—universities, psychiatric clinics, schools, and prisons. Truth itself is not outside power: every society maintains a regime of truth that defines normal versus deviant behavior. The real political task is to criticize these seemingly neutral institutions so that the obscure political violence exercised through them is unmasked and contested.

turns.speaker: Noam Chomsky
turns.text: I completely agree that institutions pretending to be neutral—corporate media, state bureaucracies, and academic technocrats—regularly mask class dominance and state violence. Yet we cannot dissolve objective truth or scientific inquiry entirely into power relations without losing the very rational standards needed to expose state propaganda! When we condemn an unjust war or expose state repression, we appeal to real factual evidence and to fundamental human needs for creative autonomy that centralized power crushes.

turns.speaker: Fons Elders
turns.text: Here we reach the core moral tension of this debate: justice versus power. Professor Chomsky, does a universal concept of justice exist beyond class interests, or, Professor Foucault, is 'justice' itself merely a weapon of power?

turns.speaker: Noam Chomsky
turns.text: If we are thinking of a decent social organization corresponding to the needs of the human essence, we envision a libertarian community in which creative initiative is free and workers control their own production without coercive state hierarchy. Of course no society has achieved absolute justice, yet we possess a rational and moral intuition of justice—grounded in human freedom, dignity, and opposition to arbitrary domination—that allows us to judge existing legal systems as fundamentally unjust and illegitimate.

turns.speaker: Michel Foucault
turns.text: One cannot prevent me from believing that these notions of 'human nature,' of 'justice,' and of the realization of human essence are all concepts formed within our Western civilization, our type of knowledge, and our philosophy, and that as a result they form part of our class system! The idea of justice itself was invented and put to work in different types of society as an instrument of a certain political and economic power—or as a weapon against that power. One cannot extrapolate these class-bound notions of justice to justify overthrowing the entire foundation of society.

turns.speaker: Fons Elders
turns.text: In our final round, let us confront the practical question of proletarian revolution and political action: if the proletariat wages a struggle against the bourgeoisie without appealing to universal justice, what prevents a victorious revolution from reproducing state terror?

turns.speaker: Michel Foucault
turns.text: When the proletariat takes power, it may well be that it exerts violent, dictatorial, and bloody power over the classes it has just conquered—and I do not see what objection one could make to that on the basis of an abstract judicial ideal! The proletariat does not wage war against the ruling class because it considers such a war 'just'; the proletariat wages war because, for the first time in history, it wants to take power. Rather than installing revolutionary courts mimicking bourgeois justice, one must dismantle the very apparatus of legal normalization.

turns.speaker: Noam Chomsky
turns.text: That is precisely where I must disagree most strongly! I would be horrified by a revolutionary movement guided solely by the desire to seize brutal dictatorial power without moral restraint or a vision of universal justice. If we must choose between trusting centralized state power and trusting free associations of libertarian socialist communities, I trust free decentralized communities—because an anarcho-syndicalist society maximizes our decent human instincts for solidarity and creativity, whereas unchecked centralized power invariably breeds terror and domination.

turns.speaker: Fons Elders
turns.text: Gentlemen, your dialogue reveals why the chasm between universal rational justice and the genealogical critique of institutional power remains one of the defining philosophical divides of our century. Thank you both for an illuminating exchange in Eindhoven.
